_about: Material options per family. mass and cost multiply the part's dry mass and price; reliability is added. The first option is the default. Densities in g/cm³, strengths in MPa, from the alloy data sheets.

options.name: Aluminium-lithium 2195
options.note: The modern tank alloy: 5 % lighter and stronger than plain aluminium. Shuttle super-lightweight tank, Falcon 9, SLS.
cons: Twice the price of plain aluminium
Bursts more easily when holed: a 1 cm debris hole can split a tank wall
options.source: Crack sizing: a tank at half its yield (about 280 MPa for 2195-T8) with K_IC about 35 MPa m^0.5 bursts once a hole reaches 2 (K_IC/sigma)^2 / pi, about 1 cm, against about 1.8 cm for 2219 or titanium and 9 cm for cryogenic stainless (Griffith-Irwin; NASA TP-2003-210788 for the hole a debris hit makes; src/builder/traits/structure.json)

options.name: Aluminium-copper 2219
options.note: The classic: Apollo, Delta II, the first Shuttle tanks. Easy to weld, cheap, a little heavier.

options.name: Stainless steel 30X
options.note: Starship's choice: heavy, cheap, and stronger when cryogenic and when red hot, so it needs less heat shielding.
pros: Takes heat and cold without complaint

options.name: Carbon-fibre composite
options.note: The lightest option; hand-laid and baked in an autoclave. It cracks instead of bending, and liquid oxygen can attack it. Electron, fairings.
options.facts: 1.6 g/cm³ · 600+ MPa along the fibres · to 120 °C
cons: Brittle: hidden cracks fail without warning

options.name: Titanium Ti-6Al-4V
options.note: Strong, light and corrosion-proof; hard to machine, so the bill is high. Pressure bottles, kick-motor cases, fittings.

options.name: Copper-alloy chamber (GRCop)
options.note: Copper carries heat away from the chamber wall into the cooling channels. The classic choice: RS-25, Merlin, Raptor.

options.name: Inconel 718 chamber
options.note: A nickel superalloy that stays strong at glowing temperatures. Long life, many restarts.

options.name: 3D-printed chamber
options.note: Laser-sintered in one piece with its channels (Rutherford, Raptor parts). Light and cheap, but porosity is hard to inspect.
options.facts: Inconel or copper powder · one piece, no welds
cons: Newer process: a little less reliable

options.name: Aluminium housing
options.note: Machined aluminium box, gold-foil insulation on top.

options.name: Radiation-hardened housing
options.note: Thicker walls and shielded electronics that shrug off solar storms.

options.name: Titanium housing
options.note: Lighter than aluminium for the same strength, and it does not care about heat.

options.name: Composite housing
options.note: Carbon-fibre panels on an aluminium frame.

options.name: Composite-overwrapped (COPV)
options.note: A thin aluminium liner wound in carbon fibre. The lightest bottle for 300 bar, and the one that failed on AMOS-6.

options.name: Titanium sphere
options.note: A forged, welded titanium ball. Heavier, and nothing hidden inside it.

options.name: Steel bottle
options.note: A plain steel pressure bottle. Heavy, cheap, utterly boring.

options.name: Steel case
options.note: Rolled and welded steel segments, as the Shuttle boosters used. Heavy and forgiving.

options.name: Graphite-epoxy case
options.note: Carbon fibre wound over a mandrel: the GEM in GEM-40. 15 % lighter.

options.name: Titanium case
options.note: A spun titanium sphere, as the Star 48 uses.
